stem: An NFA accepts a string if

options.text: At least one branch of the computation ends in an accept state
Every branch ends in an accept state

explanation: Branches that die or reject do not matter.
source: CSC 351 Formal Languages and Automata Theory.pdf, Study Session 5

stem: The ε-closure of a state is

options.text: The set of states reachable from it by ε-transitions alone, including itself

explanation: It is the first step in converting an ε-NFA.
source: CSC 351 Formal Languages and Automata Theory.pdf, Study Session 5; 2021/22 paper

stem: Every NFA can be converted into an equivalent DFA.
source: CSC 351 Formal Languages and Automata Theory.pdf, Study Session 5

stem: In the subset construction, a DFA state is final if

options.text: It contains any final state of the NFA

source: CSC 351 Formal Languages and Automata Theory.pdf, Study Session 5

stem: Which are true of an NFA?

options.text: A state may have zero, one or many arrows for a symbol
Its δ gives a set of next states
It accepts languages that no DFA can accept

explanation: NFAs and DFAs accept the same (regular) languages.
source: CSC 351 Formal Languages and Automata Theory.pdf, Study Session 5

stem: Which machine does not accept exactly the regular languages?
explanation: A PDA accepts the context-free languages.
source: CSC 351 Formal Languages and Automata Theory.pdf, Study Session 5 and 11
